ad: Rio Grande Gorge, Taos, New Mexico
nasa_ne_yapti: On 11–12 March 1971, Apollo 15 astronauts David Scott and James Irwin, with backup crew Richard Gordon and Harrison Schmitt, trained at the Rio Grande Gorge near Taos, New Mexico, the area that most closely resembled their Hadley–Apennine landing site. Driving the Grover rover simulator along the gorge rim, Scott and Irwin carried out a geologic investigation similar to the one they later made at Hadley Rille.

ciftler.metin: On 8–10 September 1971, Apollo 16 astronauts John Young and Charles Duke, with backup crew Fred Haise and Edgar Mitchell, made a geology field trip to the Rio Grande Gorge near Taos, New Mexico. On this trip they used Grover, the geologic rover built by the U.S. Geological Survey, for the first time.

nasa_ne_yapti: From 10 to 15 August 1970, Apollo 14 astronauts Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell, with backup crew Eugene Cernan and Joe Engle, made a geology field trip to the Nördlinger Ries impact crater in Germany. Their Fra Mauro landing site included the Cone Crater impact feature, so their training included impact sites on Earth.

nasa_ne_yapti: In July 1971, Apollo 16 astronauts John Young and Charles Duke explored the Sudbury Basin in Ontario, a meteorite impact structure long misinterpreted as volcanic in origin. A 2008 GSA abstract credits this training with helping them recognise the Cayley Formation at their landing site as impact breccia rather than volcanic rock.

In 1972, a year after the Apollo 16 visit, Apollo 17 astronauts Harrison Schmitt and Gene Cernan trained in Sudbury, Ontario, for the final Moon landing. Because Schmitt was a trained geologist, their visit was run as a conventional geological tour rather than the mock lunar traverse used for Apollo 16.

nasa_ne_yapti: In October 2022, NASA's Joint EVA and Human Surface Mobility Test Team used the rocky terrain of SP Crater, north of Flagstaff, Arizona, as a lunar proxy for JETT3, a series of simulated moonwalks for the Artemis III EVA study. In May 2024, the JETT5 simulation returned to the San Francisco Volcanic Field, with landing sites mapped in the SP region.

nasa_ne_yapti: NASA scientists used the Ephrata Fan in the Channeled Scabland of Washington State as an Earth analog, together with orbital data, to predict the surface of the Mars Pathfinder landing site in Ares Vallis. Golombek et al. (1999) report that the surface and the largest clasts seen at the site were similar to the predictions based on the Ephrata Fan.

nasa_ne_yapti: In May 2012, Mars Science Laboratory team members drove Scarecrow, a test rover with a full-scale copy of Curiosity's mobility system, up sandy slopes at Dumont Dunes in California's Mojave Desert. Data from its drives on windward and downwind dune slopes were to guide decisions on driving Curiosity on dunes near Mount Sharp in Gale Crater.

nasa_ne_yapti: In January 1971, the Apollo 15 crew trained at Kilbourne Hole, a crater on public land in New Mexico. They collected volcanic samples along the crater's east rim and worked as if they were on the Moon.

ciftler.metin: In January 1971, the Apollo 15 crew trained at Kilbourne Hole, a crater on public land in New Mexico. They collected volcanic samples along the crater's east rim and worked as if they were on the Moon.

In 2022, NASA's Joint EVA Test Team held its first field test, JETT1, near Kilbourne Hole by El Paso, Texas, at a site chosen for its relevance to the expected Artemis lunar terrain. The test focused on hardware development and checkout and was the first field deployment of the ExCon mockup spacesuit.

nasa_ne_yapti: In September 1972, Apollo 17 astronauts Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt carried out a practice EVA in the Lunar Crater Volcanic Field near Tonopah, Nevada, as part of their science training (Phinney, NASA SP-2015-626).

gelecek_hedef: Artemis south-polar regions (impact crater, frozen ground); Mars polar desert
nasa_ne_yapti: From 10 July to 3 August 2007, two NASA Ames K10 rovers surveyed the roughly 700 m × 700 m "Drill Hill" area inside the crater with lidar and ground-penetrating radar (CRUX GPR), with the HMP base camp acting as a lunar outpost and JSC as ground control [9]. In HMP-2010, a robotic convoy from Shackleton to Malapert was simulated with a K10 rover and the MARS-1 Humvee acting as a pressurized rover [10].

gelecek_hedef: Simple impact craters, Artemis geology training
nasa_ne_yapti: Apollo astronauts trained here from 1963 to 1970, and a tear in one astronaut's suit on the rocks led to improvements in the suit [12]. The USGS still describes the crater as an analog site [11]. An IAC-21 paper by Osinski proposes Meteor Crater, together with Mistastin, for Artemis training [30].

ad: Black Point Lava Flow, San Francisco Volcanic Field, Arizona
nasa_ne_yapti: In the Desert RATS tests of 2008–2012, with a landing site chosen on top of the flow, NASA simulated 3-, 14- and 28-day Lunar Electric Rover missions [14]. On the 14-day mission, a two-person crew drove the rover as far as Colton Crater and SP Crater [14]. NASA Earth Observatory reported on the late-2009 test [13].

ad: Mauna Kea, Pu'u Hiwahine (PISCES site), Hawaii
nasa_ne_yapti: From 27 January to 11 February 2010, NASA ran an ISRU analog test here with CSA, DLR and NORCAT, operated by PISCES, in which KSC's RESOLVE prototype simulated prospecting for volatiles at a lunar pole [16][17]. In 2012, a robotic polar mission was simulated and RESOLVE was tested again on a CSA rover [16]. In November 2009, experiments to extract oxygen from regolith were run at the same site [18].

ad: Craters of the Moon, Idaho (Inferno Chasm)
nasa_ne_yapti: The Ames-led FINESSE project, under SSERVI, worked here in 2014 and 2015 [19]. The team mapped volcanic landforms with LiDAR, differential GPS and drones and compared them with LRO NAC images and terrain models [19][20]. Operations concepts (ConOps) for future human–robotic exploration were also tested [20].

Geology training here is run by the CSA and Western University (Osinski), and NASA astronauts take part [22][30]. Kutryk (CSA) and Dominick (NASA) trained here in September 2021, and Hansen and Gibbons (CSA) with Koch and Chari (NASA) in September 2023 [22][23]. NASA's July 2024 PAC presentation lists "Fieldwork – Kamestastin" as a step in Artemis II training [24].

ad: Iceland, north of Vatnajökull National Park
gelecek_hedef: Basalt, breccia, icy ground; Artemis astronaut geology training
nasa_ne_yapti: From 24 July to 6 August 2024, the Artemis II crew (Wiseman, Glover, Koch, Hansen) and their backups (Douglas, Gibbons) received NASA-led field training north of Vatnajökull National Park [25][26]. They carried out daytime traverses and night traverses in low-angle light and tested sampling tools [25].

PANGAEA is ESA's mission, not NASA's; since 2016 it has trained ESA, NASA, JAXA and Roscosmos astronauts, and one part of the programme takes place at the Ries [27]. NASA astronauts take part; NASA astronaut Jasmin Moghbeli was one of the participants of the 10th edition in 2026 [28].

NASA Ames's ARADS project, funded by PSTAR, tested a Mars-prototype drill, a sample-transfer arm and the SOLID (CAB, Spain) and WCL instruments together here [31][32]. In September 2019, the rover drove on its own to the "Playa" site and collected samples, with commands sent twice a day [32]. The site has been studied as a Mars analog since 2003 [33].

gelecek_hedef: Meridiani Planum: jarosite, hematite, Fe-S minerals
nasa_ne_yapti: MARTE, a joint project of NASA Ames and Spain's CAB funded by ASTEP, ran from 2003 to 2005 [35]. In 2005, a one-month robotic dry-drilling mission was simulated at the edge of the open-pit mine at Peña de Hierro, and the science teams were not given prior knowledge of the site [35][37].

gelecek_hedef: Phoenix site, ground ice of northern plains
nasa_ne_yapti: Over three austral summers starting in 2009, the ASTEP-funded IceBite project (McKay, Ames) tested drills for reaching the ice beneath "dry permafrost" for a future Mars polar mission [40][42]. During the International Polar Year, Phoenix science questions were tested here (Tamppari et al. 2012) [41].

AMASE is a Norwegian-led expedition funded by NASA ASTEP and ESA, with teams from JPL, Ames and GSFC [43]. In 2009, two instruments for MSL and four for ExoMars were tested on JPL's FIDO rover [43][44].

In 2018–2019, NASA Ames's PSTAR-funded BRAILLE project ran a three-week mission here [45]. The CaveR rover was driven into Valentine Cave under a planetary mission plan, the cave was mapped with a laser scanner, and samples were taken from 9 caves [45].

ad: Pavilion Lake, British Columbia (Canada) — operations analog only, not matched
nasa_ne_yapti: The Pavilion Lake Research Project ran from 2004 to 2015 (Lim, Ames; CSA's CARN programme) and simulated science-driven EVA with DeepWorker submersibles [47]. In 2015 (PLRP-3), EVA under communication delay was tested [47].
